title: Amazon EKS: Build and Run a Cluster
subtitle: VPC, eksctl, access, compute, add-ons, load balancing and cleanup
description: Build a real Amazon EKS cluster step by step: understand what AWS manages, plan a VPC, create the cluster with eksctl, secure access with IAM, add compute with node groups and Karpenter, install add-ons, expose apps with ALB and NLB, and clean up to avoid costs.
outcomes: Explain the EKS shared-responsibility model, pricing and version support
Create a cluster in a tagged VPC from an eksctl ClusterConfig
Grant IAM principals access with access entries and map them to RBAC
Run workloads on managed nodes, Spot and Karpenter and expose them through ALB/NLB, then delete everything cleanly

modules.title: Foundations: EKS and your first cluster
modules.summary: Understand EKS, plan the VPC and create the cluster.

lessons.title: What you will build and what EKS is
lessons.summary: The path through the course, what AWS manages in EKS versus what you own, the architecture, pricing and the version support policy.
objectives: Describe the end-state cluster you will build in this course and the order of the lessons
Separate what AWS operates (control plane) from what you operate (nodes, add-ons, workloads)
Estimate the fixed and variable cost of an EKS cluster
Explain the 14+12 month version support policy and plan an upgrade cadence

sections.title: What you will build and the path through this course
sections.body:
By the end of this course you will have a real **Amazon EKS** cluster in `us-east-1`: created from a version-controlled YAML file, reachable with `kubectl`, running on managed nodes, exposing an application through an **Application Load Balancer** with HTTPS, and torn down completely so it stops costing money. Seven lessons get you there in order: (1) what EKS is, (2) a VPC and the cluster itself, (3) who is allowed to talk to it, (4) where pods run, (5) how pods get IPs and which add-ons you need, (6) how traffic enters, (7) a full deployment and cleanup.

Each lesson builds on the previous one, so follow them in sequence. You should already know Pods, Deployments and Services from `k8s-workloads`. You also need an AWS account you can spend a few dollars in. Every command that creates AWS resources is paired with the command that deletes them.

sections.title: The idea: AWS runs the brain, you run the muscle
sections.body:
A Kubernetes cluster has a **control plane** (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) and **worker nodes** that run your pods. In **Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)** AWS operates the control plane for you: it runs at least two API server instances and three etcd members across three Availability Zones (AZs), patches them, backs them up and replaces failed ones. You never see those machines; you only get an HTTPS endpoint.

Everything else is still yours: the VPC, the worker nodes, the add-ons that run inside the cluster, IAM permissions, the workloads and their cost. EKS is certified Kubernetes, so `kubectl`, Helm and your manifests work unchanged. The AWS-specific parts are authentication (IAM), networking (the VPC CNI) and storage and load balancers (EBS, ELB).

sections.title: About this example: the architecture at a glance
sections.body: This text diagram shows what exists in your AWS account once an EKS cluster is running. The control plane lives in an AWS-owned VPC; EKS attaches **cross-account ENIs** into subnets of your VPC so the API server can reach your nodes and your nodes can reach the API server. Read it from top to bottom: the dashed boundary is the ownership line, and everything below it is billed to you directly.

sections.title: About this example: listing versions and the support policy
sections.body: The command below asks the EKS API which Kubernetes versions exist and when each one leaves support. We use `describe-cluster-versions` because the support dates change, so you should read them from AWS rather than memorise them. The rules: standard support lasts 14 months, then 12 months of extended support at $0.60/hour; upgrades go one minor version at a time, control plane first, nodes after; nodes may lag the control plane by up to three minors; downgrades are impossible. In the output, compare `status` (STANDARD_SUPPORT, EXTENDED_SUPPORT) with `endOfStandardSupportDate` and `endOfExtendedSupportDate` to schedule upgrades.

sections.title: Check supported EKS versions
sections.note: Dates shown are illustrative; always query your account for the real ones.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Thinking EKS patches your nodes automatically.** With managed node groups you must start the AMI update; with self-managed nodes you do everything. **Ignoring the version clock.** Staying on an old minor version silently moves you to extended support and 6x control-plane cost. **Forgetting NAT and load balancers** when estimating cost: a tiny dev cluster can cost more in NAT gateways than in EC2.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: EKS gives you a managed, highly available Kubernetes control plane for a flat hourly fee; you own the VPC, nodes, add-ons, access and workloads. Versions get 14 months of standard support, then 12 months of paid extended support, and upgrades move one minor version at a time. In the next lesson you prepare the AWS tooling, design a VPC with correctly tagged subnets and create your first cluster with `eksctl`.

lessons.title: A VPC for EKS and creating the cluster with eksctl
lessons.summary: Prepare the tools, plan a VPC with correctly tagged subnets, NAT and endpoints, then create a cluster from a ClusterConfig file.
objectives: Install and verify aws, eksctl and kubectl and the IAM permissions they need
Plan a VPC with public and private subnets, CIDR sizes, NAT and VPC endpoints
Apply the subnet tags that load balancers rely on
Write an eksctl ClusterConfig and create, inspect and verify a cluster

sections.title: Prerequisites and how to plan the network
sections.body:
You need three command-line tools: the **AWS CLI v2** (talks to AWS APIs), **eksctl** (a CLI from Weaveworks and AWS that generates CloudFormation stacks for EKS) and **kubectl** (within one minor version of your cluster). Authenticate with `aws configure sso` or environment credentials, and verify with `aws sts get-caller-identity`. The IAM identity creating the cluster needs permissions for EKS, EC2, IAM roles and CloudFormation; for a lab, `AdministratorAccess` in a sandbox account is simplest, and the creator becomes the first cluster admin.

EKS needs a **VPC** (your private network) with subnets in **at least two AZs**; production uses three. Use **private subnets** for nodes and pods, **public subnets** only for load balancers and NAT gateways. A **NAT gateway** lets private nodes reach the internet (image pulls, AWS APIs) without being reachable; place one per AZ for resilience or one total for cost in dev. **VPC endpoints** (PrivateLink) reach AWS services without NAT: add `ecr.api`, `ecr.dkr`, `sts`, `logs` and `ec2` interface endpoints plus the `s3` gateway endpoint to save NAT charges and keep traffic private. Because every pod consumes a VPC IP, **size subnets generously**: a /19 (8,190 IPs) per private AZ is a common choice, in a /16 VPC.

sections.title: About this example: the eksctl ClusterConfig
sections.body: This is an `eksctl` config file, not a Kubernetes manifest, so it is applied with `eksctl create cluster -f`, never `kubectl apply`. It describes the cluster name, region and version, lets eksctl create a new VPC with one NAT gateway, enables the IAM OIDC provider for service-account roles, turns on control-plane logging and defines one managed node group. Look at `vpc.nat.gateway` (cost versus resilience), `privateNetworking` (nodes in private subnets) and `accessConfig` (the modern access-entry authentication mode).

sections.title: cluster.yaml (eksctl ClusterConfig)
sections.code:
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: opsdeck-eks
  region: us-east-1
  version: "1.33"
  tags:
    env: lab
    owner: platform-team
vpc:
  cidr: 10.0.0.0/16
  nat:
    gateway: Single        # HighlyAvailable = one per AZ (production)
  clusterEndpoints:
    publicAccess: true
    privateAccess: true
accessConfig:
  authenticationMode: API_AND_CONFIG_MAP
iam:
  withOIDC: true
cloudWatch:
  clusterLogging:
    enableTypes: ["api", "audit", "authenticator"]
    logRetentionInDays: 14
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: general
    instanceType: m6i.large
    minSize: 2
    desiredCapacity: 3
    maxSize: 5
    volumeSize: 50
    privateNetworking: true
    amiFamily: AmazonLinux2023
    labels: { role: general }
sections.note: eksctl creates the VPC, the subnets with the tags from the table above, the cluster IAM role and the node role for you.

sections.title: About this example: creating the cluster
sections.body: `eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml` turns the file into CloudFormation stacks: first the cluster stack (VPC, control plane, roles), then a node group stack. It takes roughly 15 to 20 minutes and prints each step. The final lines tell you that eksctl wrote credentials into `~/.kube/config` and that nodes are `Ready`; the `--dry-run` flag prints the full expanded config without creating anything, which is useful for review.

sections.title: About this example: verifying the new cluster
sections.body: After creation, check the cluster from both sides: `aws eks describe-cluster` shows what AWS knows (status, version, endpoint, VPC) and `kubectl` shows what Kubernetes sees (nodes, system pods). Look for `ACTIVE`, the endpoint URL, `v1.33.x-eks-...` on the nodes and for CoreDNS, `aws-node` and `kube-proxy` pods in `kube-system`; these are the default add-ons covered in a later lesson.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Subnets too small.** A /24 private subnet holds about 250 IPs and a few dozen pods per node exhaust it; scaling then fails with IP shortage. **Untagged public subnets**, so the load balancer controller cannot pick subnets. **Nodes in public subnets** with public IPs by accident. **Forgetting the single NAT gateway is a single point of failure** for one AZ's outbound traffic. **Using an old kubectl**: stay within one minor version of the cluster.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: You planned a /16 VPC with tagged public and private subnets, understood why NAT and VPC endpoints matter, wrote a `ClusterConfig`, created the cluster in about 15 to 20 minutes and verified it from AWS and from Kubernetes. The cluster costs money from now on, so remember the cleanup lesson. Next you will see how `kubectl` authenticated against it, and how to give teammates and CI systems access safely.

lessons.title: Access and authentication: kubeconfig, access entries and RBAC
lessons.summary: How kubectl authenticates with IAM, how to grant access with access entries (and the legacy aws-auth ConfigMap), and how endpoint access modes work.
objectives: Explain the token flow from aws eks get-token to the API server
Generate a kubeconfig with aws eks update-kubeconfig
Grant IAM principals cluster access with access entries and access policies, and know when aws-auth still appears
Bind IAM-mapped groups to Kubernetes RBAC and choose a cluster endpoint access mode

sections.title: How authentication and authorization work on EKS
sections.body:
EKS splits identity into two steps. **Authentication** answers "who are you?" using **IAM**: `kubectl` runs `aws eks get-token`, which produces a short-lived bearer token (a pre-signed STS `GetCallerIdentity` request). The API server hands it to the AWS authenticator, which resolves it to an IAM role or user ARN. **Authorization** answers "what may you do?" using Kubernetes **RBAC** (or EKS access policies, which are managed RBAC). So an IAM identity with no mapping to Kubernetes can authenticate but is denied everything.

The API server's network exposure is the **endpoint access mode**: **public only** (reachable from the internet, restricted by `publicAccessCidrs`), **public and private** (nodes use a private endpoint through the VPC, humans use the public one), or **private only** (reachable only from inside the VPC, a VPN or Direct Connect; best for production). The default is public. For a lab, public with your IP in `publicAccessCidrs` is a good balance.

sections.title: About this example: generating a kubeconfig
sections.body: A **kubeconfig** is the file `kubectl` reads to learn the server URL, the certificate authority and how to get credentials. `aws eks update-kubeconfig` writes a cluster, user and context entry into `~/.kube/config` with an `exec` credential plugin that calls `aws eks get-token`. In the output of `kubectl config get-contexts` the `*` marks the current context; `kubectl auth whoami` (Kubernetes 1.28+) shows the username Kubernetes derived from your IAM ARN.

sections.title: Create the kubeconfig and check your identity
sections.code:
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name opsdeck-eks --region us-east-1 --alias opsdeck
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*'

sections.title: About this example: granting a platform role access
sections.body: These commands create an access entry for the IAM role `PlatformAdmins` and attach the AWS-managed admin policy scoped to the whole cluster, then give a read-only role view access in a single namespace. Look at `--type STANDARD`, the `--policy-arn` values (the `AmazonEKS*Policy` family) and `--access-scope`, which is either `cluster` or `namespace`. The final `list-associated-access-policies` call confirms what each principal can do.

sections.title: Create access entries and attach policies
sections.code:
aws eks create-access-entry --cluster-name opsdeck-eks \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/PlatformAdmins --type STANDARD

aws eks associate-access-policy --cluster-name opsdeck-eks \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/PlatformAdmins \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy \
  --access-scope type=cluster

aws eks create-access-entry --cluster-name opsdeck-eks \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/Developers --type STANDARD
aws eks associate-access-policy --cluster-name opsdeck-eks \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/Developers \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSViewPolicy \
  --access-scope type=namespace,namespaces=shop

aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name opsdeck-eks

sections.title: About this example: mapping a group to your own RBAC
sections.body: Managed policies cover common cases. For finer control, create the access entry with `--kubernetes-groups deployers` and write a normal `ClusterRole` and `ClusterRoleBinding` for the group `deployers`. The manifest below lets that group manage Deployments and read Pods in the cluster; see `subjects` (kind Group, name matching the access entry) and `rules` (verbs on resources). Apply with `kubectl apply -f`, then test with `kubectl auth can-i --as-group deployers --as ci`.

sections.title: ClusterRole and binding for the deployers group
sections.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: deployer
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments", "replicasets"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: deployers-bind
subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: deployers
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: deployer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
sections.output:
clusterrole.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/deployer created
clusterrolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/deployers-bind created

$ kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as ci --as-group deployers
yes
$ kubectl auth can-i delete nodes --as ci --as-group deployers

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Editing `aws-auth` by hand** and breaking the YAML, which can lock out every user; prefer access entries. **Granting `system:masters`** as a group, which bypasses RBAC and cannot be restricted. **Binding groups with names starting `system:`**, which EKS rejects. **Sharing the cluster-creator credentials.** The creator IAM identity has hidden admin rights unless you disable `bootstrapClusterCreatorAdminPermissions`. **Opening `0.0.0.0/0`** on the public endpoint of a production cluster.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: `kubectl` authenticates with IAM tokens from `aws eks get-token`, and Kubernetes authorises with RBAC. Access entries are the modern, auditable way to map IAM roles to cluster permissions, using managed policies or groups bound to your own roles; `aws-auth` is legacy. The endpoint access mode controls who can even reach the API server. With access sorted, the next lesson adds capacity: managed node groups, Fargate and Karpenter.

lessons.title: Compute: managed node groups, Fargate and Karpenter
lessons.summary: Choose between managed node groups, Fargate and Karpenter, size instances sensibly and pick the right AMI.
objectives: Compare managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Fargate, Karpenter and EKS Auto Mode
Define managed node groups (on-demand and Spot) and a Fargate profile in eksctl
Write a Karpenter NodePool and EC2NodeClass and explain how it provisions nodes
Select instance sizes and AMI families, and understand node update strategies

sections.title: Where do pods actually run?
sections.body: A pod needs a machine. On EKS that machine is an EC2 instance (a **node**), or, with Fargate, an isolated micro-VM that AWS runs for exactly one pod. You have five options. **Managed node groups** are Auto Scaling groups that EKS creates and upgrades for you; they are the default starting point. **Self-managed nodes** are your own ASGs and AMIs, needed only for special requirements. **Fargate** runs each pod in its own VM with no nodes to manage, billed per vCPU and memory of the pod. **Karpenter** is an open-source autoscaler that launches the right-sized EC2 instance when pods are unschedulable and removes it when it is empty. **EKS Auto Mode** is a fully managed variant of compute, networking and storage components, built around Karpenter concepts.

head: Option
You manage
Scales by
Best for
Limits
rows: Instance types, scaling bounds, AMI updates
One instance family mix per group
Isolated or bursty jobs, no node ops
No DaemonSets, no GPUs, no privileged pods, EBS volumes not supported
Needs a small managed node group or Fargate to run itself

sections.title: About this example: node groups and a Fargate profile
sections.body: This extends the `ClusterConfig` from lesson 2 (apply new groups with `eksctl create nodegroup -f` and `eksctl create fargateprofile -f`). It defines an on-demand group for steady services, a Spot group with several interchangeable instance types for fault-tolerant work and a tainted group so only tolerating pods land there. The Fargate profile selects pods in the namespace `batch` that carry the label `compute: fargate`. Look at `instanceTypes` (more types means better Spot availability), `taints` and `selectors`.

sections.title: nodegroups.yaml (eksctl)
sections.code:
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: opsdeck-eks
  region: us-east-1
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: general-od
    instanceType: m6i.large
    minSize: 2
    maxSize: 6
    desiredCapacity: 3
    privateNetworking: true
    amiFamily: AmazonLinux2023
    labels: { workload: general }
  - name: spot-workers
    instanceTypes: ["m6i.large", "m5.large", "m6a.large", "m5a.large"]
    spot: true
    minSize: 0
    maxSize: 10
    desiredCapacity: 2
    privateNetworking: true
    labels: { workload: batch, lifecycle: spot }
    taints:
      - key: lifecycle
        value: spot
        effect: NoSchedule
fargateProfiles:
  - name: batch-fargate
    selectors:
      - namespace: batch
        labels: { compute: fargate }
sections.note: Pods for the spot group need a toleration for lifecycle=spot:NoSchedule and may use nodeSelector workload=batch.

sections.title: About this example: Karpenter resources
sections.body: Karpenter v1 is configured with two custom resources. The **EC2NodeClass** says how nodes are built: the AMI family (`alias: al2023@latest`), the node IAM role, and which subnets and security groups to use (found via the `karpenter.sh/discovery` tag). The **NodePool** says which nodes are allowed: instance categories, architecture, Spot or on-demand, a CPU limit for the whole pool and when to consolidate. These are CRDs created by the Karpenter Helm chart, so they are shown as plain files; apply them with `kubectl apply -f` once Karpenter runs.

sections.title: karpenter-nodepool.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: karpenter.k8s.aws/v1
kind: EC2NodeClass
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  amiSelectorTerms:
    - alias: al2023@latest
  role: KarpenterNodeRole-opsdeck-eks
  subnetSelectorTerms:
    - tags: { karpenter.sh/discovery: opsdeck-eks }
  securityGroupSelectorTerms:
    - tags: { karpenter.sh/discovery: opsdeck-eks }
  blockDeviceMappings:
    - deviceName: /dev/xvda
      ebs: { volumeSize: 50Gi, volumeType: gp3, encrypted: true }
---
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      requirements:
        - { key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: ["spot", "on-demand"] }
        - { key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category, operator: In, values: ["c", "m", "r"] }
        - { key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-generation, operator: Gt, values: ["5"] }
        - { key: kubernetes.io/arch, operator: In, values: ["amd64", "arm64"] }
      expireAfter: 720h
  limits:
    cpu: "100"
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 1m

NAME                         NODECLASS   NODES   READY   AGE

$ kubectl scale deployment inflate --replicas=10
$ kubectl get nodeclaims

default-7x2kq   c6a.2xlarge  spot       us-east-1b   ip-10-0-77-31.ec2.internal    True    52s

sections.title: Instance sizing and AMI families
head: Choice
Guidance
Example
rows: Balanced CPU and memory; start here
Fewer large nodes waste less per-node overhead; too large increases blast radius. 4 to 16 vCPU is common
Set by ENIs and IPs (see add-ons lesson)
Default for new clusters; AL2 AMIs are not published for 1.33+
Up to 20% cheaper per performance; images must be multi-arch

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Running a Spot node group with a single instance type**, so one capacity shortage stops scaling. **Forgetting tolerations** for tainted nodes; pods stay Pending with `untolerated taint`. **Putting Karpenter on nodes it manages**; run it on a small managed node group or Fargate. **Setting no NodePool `limits`**, allowing a runaway workload to launch hundreds of instances. **Requests too low**: autoscalers decide using pod resource requests, not actual usage.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: You can now choose compute deliberately: managed node groups for a stable baseline, Spot groups for tolerant work, Fargate for isolated pods and Karpenter to launch right-sized instances on demand. AL2023 or Bottlerocket are the AMIs to choose. Nodes are only useful if pods can get network addresses and cluster components run, which is the subject of the next lesson on add-ons and pod IPs.

lessons.title: EKS add-ons and how pods get VPC IP addresses
lessons.summary: Manage VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy and the EBS CSI driver as EKS add-ons, and understand pod IP allocation, max pods and prefix delegation.
objectives: Explain what each core add-on does and how EKS manages its versions
Install the EBS CSI driver add-on with EKS Pod Identity and provision a gp3 volume
Calculate the default maximum pods per node from ENIs and IPs
Enable prefix delegation to raise the pod density per node

sections.title: Add-ons and the VPC CNI idea
sections.body:
An **EKS add-on** is a piece of operational software (networking, DNS, storage, observability) that AWS packages, tests against your Kubernetes version and installs or upgrades through the EKS API. Three are present on every cluster: **vpc-cni** (the `aws-node` DaemonSet), **coredns** and **kube-proxy**. You add **aws-ebs-csi-driver** for persistent volumes and **eks-pod-identity-agent** for pod IAM roles.

The key difference from many clusters is networking: the **Amazon VPC CNI** plugin gives each pod a **real IP address from your VPC subnet**. It does this by attaching secondary **ENIs** (elastic network interfaces) to the node and handing their secondary IP addresses to pods. Pods are therefore directly routable inside the VPC and visible to security groups, but they consume subnet IPs and each instance type has a hard limit on ENIs and IPs per ENI.

sections.title: The core add-ons
head: Add-on
What it runs
Why you need it
IAM role needed?
rows: Pod networking, VPC IPs, network policy agent
Node role is enough; Pod Identity recommended for IPv6
Implements Service virtual IPs on each node

sections.title: About this example: managing add-ons with the AWS CLI
sections.body: These commands show the add-on lifecycle. First `describe-addon-versions` lists which versions are compatible with Kubernetes 1.33. Then we install the Pod Identity agent, create an IAM role trusted by `pods.eks.amazonaws.com` and associate it with the EBS CSI service account, and install the driver. Finally `update-addon` turns on **prefix delegation** for the VPC CNI. Watch the `status` field (`CREATING`, `ACTIVE`, `UPDATING`) and the `--resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE` flag, which replaces fields you edited by hand.

sections.title: Install the EBS CSI driver and enable prefix delegation
sections.code:
aws eks describe-addon-versions --addon-name aws-ebs-csi-driver --kubernetes-version 1.33 \
  --query 'addons[0].addonVersions[0].addonVersion' --output text

aws eks create-addon --cluster-name opsdeck-eks --addon-name eks-pod-identity-agent
aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name opsdeck-eks \
  --namespace kube-system --service-account ebs-csi-controller-sa \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/EbsCsiDriverRole
aws eks create-addon --cluster-name opsdeck-eks --addon-name aws-ebs-csi-driver

aws eks update-addon --cluster-name opsdeck-eks --addon-name vpc-cni \
  --configuration-values '{"env":{"ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION":"true","WARM_PREFIX_TARGET":"1"}}' \
  --resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE
aws eks list-addons --cluster-name opsdeck-eks
sections.note: The role EbsCsiDriverRole needs the AWS-managed policy AmazonEBSCSIDriverPolicy and a trust policy for pods.eks.amazonaws.com.

sections.title: About this example: a gp3 StorageClass and a claim
sections.body: With the CSI driver installed, a **StorageClass** tells Kubernetes how to create volumes: provisioner `ebs.csi.aws.com`, type `gp3`, encrypted, and `WaitForFirstConsumer` so the volume is created in the same AZ as the pod. The PersistentVolumeClaim asks for 10Gi from that class, and the Pod mounts it. Apply the file, then watch the PVC change from `Pending` (waiting for a consumer) to `Bound`. Remember an EBS volume lives in one AZ and attaches to one node at a time.

sections.title: gp3 StorageClass, claim and pod
sections.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: writer
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo hello > /data/hello.txt && sleep 3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: data

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Running out of subnet IPs** because pods and nodes share the subnet: use larger subnets or a secondary CIDR with custom networking. **Expecting prefix delegation to work on old nodes**: it needs Nitro instances and only affects newly launched nodes, so roll your node groups after enabling it. **Fragmented subnets**: prefix delegation needs free contiguous /28 blocks. **Missing `WaitForFirstConsumer`**, which can create the volume in a different AZ from the pod and leave it unschedulable. **Forgetting the IAM role for the EBS CSI driver**; PVCs stay Pending with `AccessDenied` in the controller logs.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: Add-ons are AWS-tested cluster software managed through `aws eks create-addon` and `update-addon`. The VPC CNI assigns real VPC IPs to pods, so the number of pods per node is limited by ENIs and IPs unless you enable prefix delegation, and subnets must be large enough. The EBS CSI driver turns PersistentVolumeClaims into gp3 volumes. Next you will let traffic in with the AWS Load Balancer Controller.

lessons.title: Load balancing: AWS Load Balancer Controller, ALB, NLB, ExternalDNS and cert-manager
lessons.summary: Install the AWS Load Balancer Controller, expose apps through an ALB Ingress or NLB Service with annotations, and automate DNS and certificates.
objectives: Explain which AWS load balancer the controller creates for an Ingress versus a Service
Install the AWS Load Balancer Controller with Helm and an IAM role
Write ALB Ingress and NLB Service manifests with the right annotations and target type
Describe where ExternalDNS, ACM and cert-manager fit

sections.title: Getting traffic into the cluster
sections.body:
Pods have VPC IPs but are not reachable from the internet on their own. A Kubernetes **Service** of type `LoadBalancer` or an **Ingress** must be turned into a real AWS load balancer by a controller. EKS does not include that controller by default (the in-tree cloud provider would only create old Classic Load Balancers). Install the **AWS Load Balancer Controller**, which watches Ingress and Service objects and creates: an **Application Load Balancer (ALB)**, layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS with host and path routing, for each Ingress (or Ingress group); and a **Network Load Balancer (NLB)**, layer 4 TCP/UDP/TLS with static IPs, for each Service of type `LoadBalancer` that sets `loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb`.

Both support two **target types**. `ip` registers the pod IP directly, which is faster, avoids an extra hop and works with Fargate; `instance` registers node ports. Use `ip` with the VPC CNI. The controller finds subnets by the `kubernetes.io/role/elb` tags from lesson 2 and needs an IAM role to call the ELB and EC2 APIs.

sections.title: About this example: installing the controller
sections.body: These commands download the official IAM policy, create it, associate a Pod Identity role with the controller's service account and install the Helm chart from the `eks` repository. Replace the cluster name, VPC ID and region with yours. In the result, check that the `aws-load-balancer-controller` deployment shows `2/2` ready replicas; webhook errors during later Ingress creation usually mean it is not ready yet.

sections.title: Install the AWS Load Balancer Controller
sections.code:
curl -sLo iam_policy.json https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-load-balancer-controller/v2.13.0/docs/install/iam_policy.json
aws iam create-policy --policy-name AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy --policy-document file://iam_policy.json

aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name opsdeck-eks \
  --namespace kube-system --service-account aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AWSLoadBalancerControllerRole

helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts && helm repo update
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \
  -n kube-system \
  --set clusterName=opsdeck-eks --set region=us-east-1 --set vpcId=vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 \
  --set serviceAccount.name=aws-load-balancer-controller
kubectl get deployment -n kube-system aws-load-balancer-controller
sections.output:

sections.title: About this example: an ALB Ingress and an NLB Service
sections.body: This file contains a Deployment, a ClusterIP Service, an **Ingress** served by an internet-facing ALB, and a second Service of type `LoadBalancer` served by an NLB. In the Ingress, `ingressClassName: alb` selects the controller, and the annotations choose IP targets, HTTPS with an ACM certificate and an HTTP to HTTPS redirect; the NLB Service uses `loadBalancerClass` and annotations for IP targets. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f`, then `kubectl get ingress,svc` shows the load balancer DNS names after a few minutes in the `ADDRESS` and `EXTERNAL-IP` columns.

sections.title: ALB Ingress and NLB Service for the web app
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP":80},{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123456789012:certificate/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname: shop.example.com
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-nlb
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80

sections.title: ExternalDNS and cert-manager: who does what
sections.body: A load balancer DNS name like `k8s-default-web-...elb.amazonaws.com` is not something users type. **ExternalDNS** is a controller you install that watches Services and Ingresses and creates matching records in **Route 53** (an alias record from `shop.example.com` to the ALB), using the `external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname` annotation or the Ingress host. For certificates there are two models. With an ALB you usually use **AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)**: you request a public certificate, reference its ARN in the Ingress, and TLS terminates on the load balancer, with AWS renewing it. **cert-manager** is a Kubernetes add-on that issues certificates (Let's Encrypt or a private CA) as Secrets inside the cluster, which you need when TLS must terminate in the pod, for service mesh certificates or for an NGINX ingress.

sections.title: Choosing the right piece
head: Need
Use
Installed as
Notes
rows: TCP/UDP, static IPs, very high throughput
L4, preserves client IP with ip targets
Public TLS on the load balancer
TLS inside the cluster / private CA

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Missing subnet tags**, so the controller logs `couldn't auto-discover subnets` and the Ingress has no address. **Wrong certificate region**: the ACM certificate must be in the same region as the ALB. **Forgetting `target-type: ip`** with Fargate, which cannot use instance targets. **One ALB per Ingress** is costly: use `alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name` to share. **Readiness probes missing**, so new pods receive traffic before they are ready. **Leaving load balancers behind**: they are not deleted if you remove the cluster without deleting Services first.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: The AWS Load Balancer Controller turns Ingress objects into ALBs and `LoadBalancer` Services into NLBs; annotations choose scheme, targets, listeners and certificates. ExternalDNS publishes Route 53 records and ACM or cert-manager provide TLS. You now have every building block. The last lesson combines them into a complete deployment and, importantly, deletes everything in the right order.

lessons.title: Deploying a sample app end to end and cleaning up to avoid costs
lessons.summary: Deploy a production-shaped app behind an ALB on your cluster, verify it, then delete everything in the correct order.
objectives: Deploy a namespaced app with resources, probes, a PodDisruptionBudget and an ALB Ingress
Verify the rollout, load balancer and HTTP response from outside the cluster
Delete Ingresses and Services before the cluster so AWS load balancers are removed
Check for leftover billable resources after eksctl delete cluster

sections.title: Putting it all together
sections.body:
You now have each piece: a cluster (lesson 2), access (3), nodes (4), IPs and storage add-ons (5) and the load balancer controller (6). In this lesson you deploy a small but production-shaped application, `shop`, and then remove everything. The app uses a dedicated **namespace**, a Deployment with three replicas spread over nodes, resource requests and limits (so the autoscaler can make good decisions), readiness and liveness probes, a **PodDisruptionBudget** so node upgrades never take all pods down at once, and an internet-facing ALB Ingress.

The order of operations matters in both directions. Deploy: namespace, workload, service, ingress. Clean up: Ingresses and LoadBalancer Services first (so the controller deletes the AWS load balancers it created), then workloads and volumes, then add-on infrastructure, and only then the cluster.

items.title: 1. Confirm context and capacity
items.body: `kubectl config current-context` and `kubectl get nodes` show the right cluster with Ready nodes.

items.title: 2. Apply the manifests
items.body: One `kubectl apply -f shop.yaml` creates namespace, Deployment, Service, PDB and Ingress.

items.title: 3. Wait for the rollout
items.body: `kubectl rollout status` returns when all replicas are Ready.

items.title: 4. Wait for the ALB
items.body: The Ingress ADDRESS appears after 2 to 3 minutes; targets must be healthy.

items.title: 5. Test over HTTP
items.body: `curl` the ALB hostname with the Host header, or via Route 53 if ExternalDNS runs.

items.title: 6. Clean up in order
items.body: Ingress and Services, then namespace, then add-ons, then `eksctl delete cluster`.

sections.title: About this example: the shop application manifest
sections.body: This single file contains everything the app needs. Look at the Deployment's `topologySpreadConstraints` (one pod per node when possible), `resources` (requests drive scheduling and Karpenter, limits cap usage), the two probes, the PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 2` and the Ingress annotations from the previous lesson, here without a certificate so plain HTTP works in your lab. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f shop.yaml`.

sections.title: shop.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: web }
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
            limits: { memory: 256Mi }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80

sections.title: About this example: verifying the deployment
sections.body: These commands confirm each layer, from inside to outside: the rollout finished, pods are spread over different nodes (see the NODE column), the Ingress received an ALB hostname and an HTTP request returns the nginx page. If the Ingress stays without an address, `kubectl describe ingress` shows the controller events; a `502` or `503` right after creation usually means targets are still registering.

sections.title: Verify rollout, load balancer and HTTP

kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/web
kubectl -n shop get pods -o wide
kubectl -n shop get ingress web
ALB=$(kubectl -n shop get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}')
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://$ALB/

sections.title: About this example: cleaning up in the right order
sections.body: Deleting the cluster directly can leave ALBs, NLBs, security groups and ENIs behind, because Kubernetes controllers never get the chance to remove them; the leftover ENIs then block the VPC deletion. So delete the namespace (which removes the Ingress and Service and makes the controller delete the ALB), uninstall the controller, remove any PVCs so EBS volumes go away, and only then run `eksctl delete cluster`. The final two commands check that no cluster, load balancer or unattached volume remains.

sections.title: Delete the app, the cluster and verify nothing is left
sections.code:
kubectl delete namespace shop
kubectl delete pvc --all -A
helm uninstall aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system
eksctl delete cluster --name opsdeck-eks --region us-east-1 --wait
aws eks list-clusters --region us-east-1
aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --query 'LoadBalancers[].LoadBalancerName'
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available --query 'Volumes[].VolumeId'

sections.title: Cost traps after deleting the cluster
sections.body: Check these in the console or CLI: **load balancers** (`aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers`), **unattached EBS volumes** and snapshots, **NAT gateways and Elastic IPs** (created by eksctl, removed with the VPC stack), **CloudWatch log groups** `/aws/eks/opsdeck-eks/cluster` (retention keeps billing), **ECR images**, **Route 53 records** created by ExternalDNS, and **IAM roles** you created manually such as `EbsCsiDriverRole`. **Common mistakes:** deleting the CloudFormation stack by hand while resources are attached, leaving an Ingress behind so the VPC cannot be deleted, and forgetting a second cluster in another region.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: You built a cluster from a config file, secured access with IAM access entries, added managed, Spot and Karpenter capacity, installed the core add-ons and the AWS Load Balancer Controller, deployed a probe-protected, PDB-protected app behind an ALB and removed it all without leaving billable leftovers. From here, take the same design into code with Terraform, package the app with Helm, add observability and GitOps, and rehearse a version upgrade (control plane, add-ons, then nodes) in a throwaway cluster before you do it in production.

questions.question: Why delete Ingresses and LoadBalancer Services before the cluster?
options: So controllers remove the AWS load balancers they created
questions.explain: Without that, ALBs/NLBs and ENIs stay behind and block VPC deletion and keep billing.

questions.question: What does minAvailable: 2 in a PodDisruptionBudget protect against?
options: Too many voluntary evictions at once, e.g. node drains
questions.explain: PDBs limit voluntary disruptions such as node drains and upgrades.

questions.question: Which command removes the cluster created from the ClusterConfig?
questions.explain: eksctl deletes the CloudFormation stacks it created.

questions.question: Which leftover commonly keeps billing after deletion?
options: Unattached EBS volumes and CloudWatch log groups
questions.explain: Volumes and log groups are separate AWS resources with their own charges.
